Kitsault

The Town That Waited

At the head of a misty northern fjord stands a town built for 1,200 people and lived in for eighteen months — mowed, heated and empty since 1983.

  • Mine opened April 1981
  • Closed late 1982
  • Waiting ever since

Before the town

A hundred years of digging at Alice Arm

Long before a single foundation was poured at Kitsault, prospectors were already working the inlet — and the Nisga’a had named these waters centuries before that.

The name and the first claims

“Kitsault” adapts the Nisga’a Gits’oohl — “a ways in behind,” or “at the inside” of the inlets. Old records spell it a dozen ways: Kitzault, Kitzaulte, Gitzault, Chigitsoult, Kitsaulte. The neighbouring Nisga’a community of Gits’oohl, at the mouth of the Kitsault River beside Alice Arm, was formerly Gitzault Indian Reserve No. 24, rescinded as a reserve under the Nisga’a Final Agreement in 2000.

In 1910 four Scandinavian prospectors — Ole Evindsen, Ludwig Eik, Ole Pearson and E. Carlson — discovered silver up the Kitsault River Valley. Alice Arm itself was named for Alice Mary Tomlinson, wife of Reverend Robert Tomlinson, and grew into a steamer landing and post office that is mostly summer cottages today.

The Dolly Varden silver mine

The 1910 strike became the Dolly Varden silver mine, backed by Chicago money and Alfred Taylor — the man behind Park Royal Shopping Centre in West Vancouver who later built the Lions Gate Bridge. In 1919 a 17-mile narrow-gauge railway was laid from Alice Arm to the mine; when the company couldn’t pay for the railroad, the railway builders seized the mine. Between 1919 and 1921 it produced about 1.3 million ounces of silver, with regular ore grading 63 ounces to the ton and high-grade ore an astonishing 1,280.

The railway was reused for logging from 1923 to 1927, then replaced by a road in the mid-1940s. A second act came in 1947, when the eastern firm Torbrit built a 400-ton-per-day mill, a 2,000-horsepower hydro plant and a full camp with hall, schoolroom and badminton court for about $2 million. From 1948 to 1958 the mine yielded roughly 19 million ounces of silver before the ore body depleted and the price of silver sat at $0.85 an ounce. Across all eras, Dolly Varden produced about 20 million ounces. The railway was photographed by the Dominion Photo Company, 1929 film footage of it survives, and the story is told in Darryl E. Muralt’s Steel Rails and Silver Dreams. Today Dolly Varden Silver Corp is actively exploring the ground again.

Anyox, down the inlet

Down Observatory Inlet, Granby Consolidated built the company town of Anyox from 1912; by 1914 some 2,500 to 3,000 people lived there around a copper mine and smelter that also yielded gold and silver. With no road or rail, everything arrived by ocean steamer from Prince Rupert, 145 km away. The town had machine shops, a curling rink, a golf course, a hospital — and the first wooden tennis court in Canada, built in the spring of 1918. That same year the Spanish flu arrived by ship and killed dozens.

In the early 1920s John S. Eastwood built a 156-foot concrete hydro dam at Anyox, the tallest in Canada for years. A forest fire partly destroyed the town in 1923 and it was rebuilt, but on November 27, 1934 an experimental overcharged blast meant to join two open pits shattered the tunnels and fractured the rock. The mine closed on July 31, 1935 — Great Depression copper prices finished what the blast started — with 100 million pounds of copper stockpiled unsold. Equipment was salvaged for the Second World War, and a 1942 fire burned what wooden structures remained. Even the name is disputed: ‘place of hiding’ in Tsimshian, say some sources, or “hidden waters” from the Nisga’a anyoose. Today Anyox is concrete and steel ruins being reclaimed by forest, its slag pile mined for abrasives.

Molybdenum’s first act

The molybdenum deposit at Kitsault was discovered in 1911 and first diamond-drilled by Kennco Explorations in 1959. From January 1968 to April 1972 it was worked as an open pit by B.C. Molybdenum, a Kennco subsidiary: about 9.3 million tonnes of ore yielding roughly 22.9 million pounds of molybdenum, until low prices closed it. That era’s camp was modular homes and trailers, not a town — and in 1971 a landslide swept a dozen of those trailers into Alice Arm. Tugboats fished them out of the water; nobody was hurt.

The name predates all mining. Gits’oohl — “a ways in behind” — named these inlets centuries before any prospector arrived.

1978–1983

The town Amax built

In two years a wilderness head-of-fjord became a complete modern town — hospital, school, mall, pub, pool and all — ready for twelve hundred people.

The building boom ran from 1978 to 1980 at a reported cost of about $50 million, on a site variously described as 350 acres or 350 hectares of industrial land. Rick Killam served as the project administrator for the construction. The town was designed for 1,200 residents, with a stated capacity of 1,500. Housing accounts differ — the town’s own history gives roughly 100 single-family homes and duplexes plus seven apartment buildings with about 200 suites, while newspaper reports have put it at 90 homes plus 210 apartments, or 90 houses plus 150 apartment units — but the picture is the same: a full community, raised from nothing.

And what a community. A modern hospital — Amax recruited a doctor before the access road was even finished. A school, which opened its doors to find the children had made giant cardboard cutouts of swimmers, goggles and fins, to hang from the swimming-pool ceiling. A shopping mall with a Sears outlet, a supermarket, the Knight & Day restaurant, a Royal Bank branch, a post office, the Maple Leaf Pub, a movie theatre, two recreation centres with jacuzzis, saunas and a theatre, a swimming pool, a library holding thousands of books, a curling rink and a bowling alley. Underground phone lines and TV cable. Sewage systems. Water the town’s own history calls the cleanest running water in all of British Columbia.

Families began moving in during 1980. The mine itself opened in April 1981, after what one account calls “much fanfare, controversy and financial investment.” About 400 of the town’s roughly 1,000 residents worked at the open pit; across its 1981–82 operating life it processed some 4.08 million tonnes of ore for nearly 9 million pounds of saleable molybdenum.

A correction that matters

Many secondary articles say Phelps Dodge built Kitsault. That is wrong. Amax of Canada built the town in 1978–80 and ran the mine in 1981–82. Phelps Dodge only came into the picture in 1999, when it acquired Cyprus Amax — itself the product of Amax’s 1993 merger with Cyprus Minerals — and inherited the property. It was an affiliate of Phelps Dodge that sold the town in 2004/05; Phelps Dodge was itself acquired by Freeport-McMoRan in 2007. The error is repeated so widely that it is worth stating plainly: the town is Amax’s.

Late 1982

The price that killed it

Molybdenum is a steel-hardening alloy metal, prized for strength, hardness and corrosion resistance. In late 1982, in the teeth of the 1982 recession and a flood of byproduct molybdenum pouring out of copper mines, its price free-fell from roughly $30 a pound to $1.69.

The mine closed after about eighteen months of operation. One account has the town completely empty by July 1983; another says the end of 1983. Either way, some 1,200 people left a town that was barely two years old — and it was Amax’s second Kitsault closure for exactly the same reason: the B.C. Molybdenum pit of 1968–72 had also shut on low prices.

From about $30 a pound to $1.69. Eighteen months of operation, and the gates were locked.

1979

The tailings fight

Before the mine even opened, its waste plan set off one of the sharpest environmental battles in British Columbia’s mining history.

In 1979 the federal Cabinet granted Amax a controversial dispensation: permission to dump mine tailings directly into Alice Arm — up to 100 million tonnes over 26 years. The Nisga’a, who had not been consulted, led the fight against it as a threat to the fishery, backed by churches, environmentalists and the BC Federation of Labour. The protest was carried all the way to the Amax shareholders’ meeting in New York.

The language was fierce. MP Jim Fulton called the dumping “akin to genocide.” Construction administrator Rick Killam remembered the newspaper headline that summed up the fear for the inlet’s crab fishery: “King Crabs Flee Alice Arm.”

The protest ended when the mine closed in late 1982. Years later, a provincial mining-law timeline found that the Kitsault mine, the Dolly Varden mine and the Anyox smelter had all impacted Alice Arm — a 2010 finding that put the old controversy back on the record.

1983–2005

The long sleep

For two decades a fully built town sat empty at the head of the fjord — kept heated, mowed and waiting, just in case the mine ever came back.

The mine stayed on care and maintenance until 1996, when reclamation planning began — decommissioning, site preparation, revegetation. The town was kept heated and maintained throughout as a restart asset, at a reported cost of about $400,000 a year.

From 1986 until about 2004, Kitsault had exactly two full-time residents: John and Patricia Wheatley — he the former mine manager, she his wife — living alone in a town built for 1,500. In summer they kept up the lawns, the roads and the water lines, and kept the pool full. In winter they plowed and kept the mall, the hospital and the recreation centre heated. In summer they made a monthly supply run to Terrace; the road was closed from October to June — seven months of the year. They canned food for winter, fished halibut, king crab and salmon, watched bears at the basement window, and drove with ravens flying alongside the truck. They retired to Houston around 2004.

The town was put on the market: listed in the early 1990s at $23 million, and former Nisga’a president Joe Gosnell says the Nisga’a offered $10 million and were refused. In 2004 it was listed with Niho Land & Cattle at $7 million — and that September, the whole town was listed for sale on eBay at about the same price. Rick Killam, who had overseen its construction, said of the abandonment: “It was heartbreaking for the people who lived there.”

In 1999, while the town slept, a documentary called Ghost Towns of Alice Arm and Kitsault put its story on film.

Two people. A town built for 1,500. Eighteen years of lawns, plowing, and bears at the basement window. — the Wheatleys, Kitsault’s only full-time residents, 1986–~2004

2004/2005–today year and price disputed — see Open questions

A new owner

In the mid-2000s a Virginia medical-supply entrepreneur bought the entire town — and has kept it standing ever since.

The man

Krishnan Suthanthiran was born in 1947 in southern India, to grocery-store owners. He earned a bachelor’s degree in engineering in Coimbatore in 1969 and immigrated to Canada that September with $400, taking a master’s in mechanical engineering at Carleton University in Ottawa in 1971 on a National Research Council assistantship. He moved to Washington, DC in 1972 and worked as an engineer-physicist at Freedmen’s Hospital, later Howard University Hospital, under the oncologist Dr. Ulrich K. Henschke. His father had died of colon cancer in 1968 — the turn that aimed his life at cancer medicine.

In 1977 he founded Best Medical International in Springfield, Virginia, a medical-supplies and devices company that grew into the TeamBest family of companies. He later founded the Brachytherapy Research and Educational Foundation (1987) and the non-profit Best Cure Foundation (2007), and in 2009 bought Best Theratronics of Kanata, Ontario. He has also founded three political parties — Proud Indian (2013), Proud American (2020) and Proud Canadian (2021). He is a US citizen and lives in Springfield, Virginia.

The purchase

The sale’s year and price are both disputed. Sources cite $5 million cash (Gizmodo, citing CBC) in 2004; $5.7 million US (Wikipedia, citing CBC, and Canadian Geographic) in 2004 or 2005, with the Washington Post reporting he offered it sight unseen after reading a news story; and about $7 million (the Globe and Mail in 2014, reporting 2005) — a figure Suthanthiran himself repeated in 2026, saying he spent “about US$7 million” some two decades earlier and noting that media had cited lower numbers. He bought through his company Kitsault Resorts Ltd., and later renamed the town “Chandra Krishnan Kitsault” after his late mother.

What he has done with it

Maintenance spending is reported in escalating figures: about $2 million by 2005, $18 million over nine years to 2014, $25 million total invested by 2014 (the Globe and Mail), and more than $2 million a year (Canadian Geographic, 2026) — with 10 to 15 workers making the rounds of the homes and structures. The Wheatleys gave way to caretakers Indhu and Mathew Mathew. Indhu curated a small town museum in one of the houses — left-behind trophies lined up on the mantel — while the hospital stood frozen with beds made and IV saline bags still hanging, grocery carts sat in the empty mall, a curling stone propped open the Maple Leaf Pub door, and the VIP lodge and tea house stayed furnished as in the early 1980s.

Unrealized plans came and went: an eco-resort, an artists’ and scientists’ retreat and think tank, a movie studio, a vacation resort, a health spa and retirement community. In 2013 the pivot turned to energy.

The town today

Kitsault is immaculately maintained and empty. Lawns are mowed, heat stays on in key buildings, power is on, hospital beds are made, and the library’s thousands of books — some dating to the early 20th century — stop at 1983. Daycare toys sit in immaculate condition; a 40-year-old basketball is still inflated. Silver foxes and grizzly bears move through the streets. It is private property, closed to the general public; custom tours can be arranged through Northern BC Jet Boat Tours in Terrace.

2004/05

The sale disputed

Suthanthiran buys the town — land, roads, homes and all — via Kitsault Resorts Ltd. Reported figures range from $5M to about US$7M.

2008–10

Access dispute

Kitsault Resorts denies Avanti Mining access to the town; the BC Supreme Court rules for Avanti — the mining right-of-way stands.

2013

The energy pivot

Suthanthiran forms Kitsault Energy Ltd. and begins pitching the town as an LNG and pipeline terminal site.

2016

LNG licence

The National Energy Board grants a 20-mtpa, 20-year LNG export licence. It expires in 2024 with no exports ever made.

2021

A new name

The town is renamed “Chandra Krishnan Kitsault” for Suthanthiran’s late mother; Indhu and Mathew Mathew are its caretakers.

2026

The pitch returns

At 78, Suthanthiran is back in Calgary with glossy brochures: two pipelines and liquid-butanol exports from a marine terminal near Kitsault.

2008–today

The mine’s second life

The mineral property under the town is owned separately from the town itself — and for fifteen years, companies have been trying to bring it back.

In October 2008 Avanti Mining acquired the past-producing Kitsault molybdenum property. The studies that followed were serious. A 2008 preliminary assessment (SRK) sketched a 15-year mine producing 363 million pounds of molybdenum for $424 million in capital costs. A 2009 pre-feasibility study (Wardrop/Tetra Tech) put proven and probable reserves at 215.3 million tonnes grading 0.085% molybdenum, with 368 million pounds over 15 years, $641 million in capital, an 8%-discount net present value of $551 million and a 20.6% internal rate of return. A 2010 feasibility study (AMEC) raised that to 232.5 million tonnes at 0.081%, 373.9 million pounds over 16 years, and $770 million in capital for a 40,000-tonne-per-day open pit feeding a flotation mill.

Avanti engaged the Nisga’a from January 2008 — more than 650 engagements and over $1.3 million in engagement funding from 2009 — reached an agreement with the Nisga’a Lisims Government, and set a goal of about half of the 300 operating jobs going to Nisga’a and other First Nations people. In April 2012 it arranged up to $640 million in financing with five lenders. The project won its BC Environmental Assessment Certificate in March 2013 and federal environmental approval in June 2014.

Then the market turned again. Avanti — renamed Alloycorp — shelved the financing; capital costs had swollen toward $1.2 billion and the project needed a sustained molybdenum price of about US$10 a pound. Permits were kept in good standing. In 2021 New Moly LLC was formed, combining the Kitsault deposit with the Mt. Hope molybdenum asset in Nevada, and around 2023 five junior companies signed a memorandum to share New Moly’s permitted Kitsault mill. New Moly has said it plans to begin mining at Kitsault by the end of 2027 — that is the company’s stated aspiration, not an established fact.

2013–2026

The energy proposals

With the mine stalled, the owner has spent a decade pitching Kitsault as an energy export port on the Pacific.

In January 2013 Suthanthiran formed Kitsault Energy Ltd. and began pitching the empty town as the site of an LNG plant and pipeline terminal, with talk of a $30-billion project. The May 2014 pitch — a 14-point “Dedicated Energy Corridor and Energy Export Terminal” — leaned on what the town already had: 90 houses plus 150 condos ready to shelter about 1,000 residents, BC Hydro service, road, air and water access, deep saltwater navigation, 350 acres of fee-simple private land, regional-district tax advantages, and an existing environmental assessment.

The National Energy Board application sought to export up to 20 million tonnes per annum of LNG for 20 years — replacing an earlier 5-mtpa application — via floating LNG modules of 4 to 5 mtpa each, with first operations hoped for 2018 and a pipeline of about 600 km. Licence GL0334 was granted on May 27, 2016. It expired in 2024: no exports ever commenced, and nothing was built.

In February 2026 the Canadian Press reported Suthanthiran was pitching again — this time two pipelines from Alberta to the coast, one for natural gas and one for crude oil, with the oil and gas exported as liquid butanol from a marine terminal near Kitsault. He arrived in Calgary with glossy brochures touting the town’s housing and infrastructure, met with Alberta energy ministry staff, and framed the pitch in trade and geopolitical terms: “I truly believe that this is the right thing for Canada and this is the right thing for the First Nations.” As with every scheme before it, this is the owner’s proposal — not a project underway.

Territory

Nisga’a territory

Kitsault stands in traditional Nisga’a territory, north of the Nass Valley, beside the Nisga’a community of Gits’oohl.

The Nisga’a Final Agreement — effective May 11, 2000, the first modern treaty in British Columbia, covering about 2,000 km² of Nisga’a Lands — rescinded Gitzault Indian Reserve No. 24, the reserve that became the community of Gits’oohl at the mouth of the Kitsault River.

The Nisga’a have shaped Kitsault’s story at every turn. In 1979 they were not consulted on the Cabinet’s tailings-dumping dispensation — and they led the protest that followed. In the 1990s, former Nisga’a president Joe Gosnell says, the Nation offered $10 million for the abandoned town and was refused. The access road to Kitsault runs through Nisga’a lands, and any mine restart or energy project requires consultation under the treaty — in Gosnell’s words, “not just sending a letter.”

Honesty first

Open questions

The sources don’t agree on everything about Kitsault. Here is what is still unsettled — stated as ranges and attributions, never smoothed over.

Purchase price and year

$5 million cash (Gizmodo, citing CBC), $5.7 million US (Wikipedia/CBC 2013; Canadian Geographic 2026), or about US$7 million (the Globe and Mail, 2014; Suthanthiran himself in 2026). Year: 2004 (Wikipedia; the eBay listing) or 2005 (Globe; Yahoo; Canadian Geographic; his own bio).

Housing counts

About 100 homes and duplexes plus seven apartment buildings with ~200 suites (the town’s own site), versus 90 homes plus 210 apartments (Northword), versus 90 houses plus 150 units (the Globe and Mail). Design capacity is given as 1,500.

Land area

350 acres (Yahoo 2013; BOE Report 2014) versus 350 hectares (the Globe and Mail, 2014) — a factor of 2.5 apart.

Build cost

About $50 million is the widely reported figure for the 1978–80 construction. One low-credibility site claims $250 million; no reliable source supports it.

The date it went empty

By July 1983 (Northword) versus the end of 1983 (BOE Report). Suthanthiran has said the town was “vacant since October, 1983.”

Who built the town

Primary records say Amax of Canada, 1978–80. Many secondary articles say Phelps Dodge — they inherited it in 1999 and sold it in 2004/05. This site goes with Amax.

Unverified stories

That Amax bought the site as early as 1973 (thinly corroborated); that some houses were airlifted out, leaving foundations (a commenter anecdote); that Phelps Dodge “bought back the houses and ordered everyone to leave” (Gizmodo, uncited).

Smaller uncertainties

What “Anyox” means (‘place of hiding’ vs. “hidden waters”); the owner’s claim that Enbridge/Spectra and TC Energy approved pipelines near Kitsault (unverified); the 2027 mine-restart plan (the company’s aspiration); and Wikipedia’s stale infobox population of “1 (2008).”

Firsthand history

Memories

Did you live in Kitsault? Work at the mine, teach at the school, bowl at the alley, or ride the jet boat up Alice Arm?

A town that stood for eighteen months belongs to the people who stood in it. This is where their recollections will live — the first days of the construction boom, the winter the price fell, the long quiet years, the museum Indhu Mathew keeps, whatever only a former resident would know.

Hundreds of photographs, videos and firsthand accounts are already being shared by former residents in the Kitsault Remembered community, and material gathered there will find its home in this section and in the gallery above. If you have a memory to add, a photograph to identify, or a correction to the record, use the form below — every contribution helps this history grow.
